stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G1P1) presents to the emergency department on day 4 postpartum after a spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by a manual removal of retained placental tissue at the time of delivery. She reports 24 hours of fever, offensive-smelling vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain. She is exclusively breastfeeding without any breast concerns.

On examination the fundus is 4 finger-breadths above the symphysis pubis and boggy, with cervical excitation and marked lower abdominal tenderness. She has no signs of skin infection at the perineum. She has no known drug allergies. She has not received antibiotics since delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender, boggy, 4 fingerbreadths above symphysis; offensive lochia; cervical excitation; no perineal skin infection
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.1 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 168 mg/L (<5); lactate 3.2 mmol/L; blood cultures taken; endocervical swab sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone until formal culture sensitivity is available
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers Gram positives only and misses Gram negatives and anaerobes that dominate polymicrobial endometritis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days from ED discharge home
options.rationale: Sepsis with SIRS features and lactate above 2 requires IV therapy and admission; oral outpatient management is inadequate. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: IV amoxicillin 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg all 8-hourly
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole is the standard Australian empirical regimen for severe puerperal sepsis, covering group A strep, Gram negatives and anaerobes. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy as broad Gram negative and Gram positive cover
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy lacks reliable anaerobic cover which is essential in polymicrobial puerperal sepsis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: IV clindamycin 600 mg 8-hourly with intravenous fluids only as first-line therapy today
options.rationale: Clindamycin alone lacks adequate Gram negative cover; a triple regimen or a beta-lactam plus metronidazole is required. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

explanation.summary: Puerperal sepsis is a leading cause of maternal death worldwide. Empirical therapy must cover Group A streptococcus, Gram negatives (including E coli), Gram positives and anaerobes; Australian eTG recommends IV amoxicillin (or benzylpenicillin) plus gentamicin plus metronidazole for severe endometritis and puerperal sepsis. Retained products of conception require evacuation once the patient is stable on antibiotics. Early sepsis recognition using SIRS or qSOFA, source control and hour-1 IV antibiotics are critical.
key_points: Standard triple: amoxicillin/benzylpenicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole.
Antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition.
Look for and evacuate retained products.
Group A streptococcus can be rapidly fatal.
explanation.pearls: Postpartum sepsis with boggy uterus and offensive lochia after a manual removal needs triple IV amoxicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole within the sepsis hour bundle, then imaging for retained products.

stem:
A 26-year-old primigravida with known type 1 von Willebrand disease is reviewed at 34 weeks in the combined obstetric-haematology clinic. Her sister has the same diagnosis. She has a history of heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and prolonged bleeding after wisdom tooth extraction that responded to tranexamic acid and desmopressin.

Her third trimester coagulation screen today shows von Willebrand factor:antigen 92 IU/dL (50-150), von Willebrand factor:ristocetin cofactor activity 88 IU/dL (50-150), factor VIII activity 110 IU/dL (50-150). She has had an uncomplicated pregnancy so far. Baseline haemoglobin is 120 g/L and platelets are 240 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, foetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundal height 34 cm, no bruising, no petechiae, no active bleeding
data_table.Investigations: VWF:Ag 92 IU/dL, VWF:RCo 88 IU/dL, FVIII 110 IU/dL; Hb 120 g/L; platelets 240 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 4.8 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Recommend termination of pregnancy given the significant peripartum bleeding risk exists
options.rationale: There is no clinical indication for termination in a well-controlled type 1 vWD pregnancy with autocorrected factor levels. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Elective caesarean section at 38 weeks under general anaesthesia to avoid regional block
options.rationale: Caesarean is not indicated on haematological grounds when VWF activity is above 50; regional anaesthesia is acceptable at these levels. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Prophylactic von Willebrand factor concentrate infusion at onset of established labour
options.rationale: VWF concentrate is reserved for VWF activity under 50 IU/dL at delivery or type 2 or 3 disease; her third trimester levels have autocorrected. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Plan vaginal delivery with active third stage and prophylactic tranexamic acid at delivery
options.rationale: Type 1 vWD with third trimester VWF activity above 50 IU/dL can deliver vaginally with active third stage and prophylactic TXA, without requiring VWF concentrate. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Avoid all regional anaesthesia in labour due to unacceptable haematoma risk in this patient
options.rationale: Regional anaesthesia is safe when VWF and FVIII activity are above 50 IU/dL; blanket avoidance denies effective analgesia. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: Von Willebrand factor and factor VIII levels rise physiologically in pregnancy and often reach normal levels in type 1 vWD by the third trimester. Peripartum planning is based on VWF:RCo and FVIII activity at 34-36 weeks: above 50 IU/dL allows vaginal delivery, active third stage, and regional anaesthesia without VWF concentrate; below 50 requires DDAVP (if responsive and outside pre-eclampsia risk) or VWF concentrate at the onset of labour. Tranexamic acid can be given prophylactically for 5-7 days postpartum to reduce secondary PPH risk. Types 2 and 3 vWD, and any active bleeding, need haematologist-led planning.
key_points: VWF and FVIII rise in pregnancy; check at 34-36 weeks.
Levels above 50 IU/dL allow vaginal delivery and regional block.
TXA reduces secondary PPH in vWD.
DDAVP is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia risk.
explanation.pearls: Type 1 vWD with third trimester VWF:RCo and FVIII both above 50 IU/dL delivers vaginally with active third stage and prophylactic TXA; VWF concentrate is only needed if activity remains below 50.

sources.label: RANZCOG bleeding disorders in pregnancy statement

stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida presents at 29+3 weeks with a sudden gush of clear fluid per vagina and a steady leak since. Sterile speculum examination confirms pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix. There are no contractions on the tocograph, the CTG is reactive and there is no vaginal bleeding or foul discharge.

She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Her white cell count is normal and CRP is unremarkable. A high vaginal swab is sent for microscopy and culture; group B streptococcus status is currently unknown. She has no known drug allergies. She has completed her first dose of betamethasone in ED.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, foetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum: pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix, cervix long and closed; no active bleeding; abdomen soft, non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 5 mg/L (<5); high vaginal swab sent; CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate latency antibiotic regimen?

options.text: No antibiotics unless the patient develops fever or foetal tachycardia during the admission
options.rationale: Withholding latency antibiotics ignores the ORACLE I benefit of shorter time to delivery and lower neonatal morbidity in PPROM. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 10 days from ED admission today
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided in PPROM because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk in the ORACLE I trial. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 4 hours until membrane rupture reaches 24 hours in duration
options.rationale: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis (not latency antibiotics) is warranted with penicillin at delivery; oral erythromycin is the latency regimen. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days for anaerobic cover of the genital tract
options.rationale: Metronidazole monotherapy does not prolong pregnancy in PPROM and is not first-line for latency; erythromycin is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: Oral erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days or until delivery
options.rationale: Erythromycin latency antibiotics per ORACLE I are the AU standard for PPROM to prolong pregnancy and reduce neonatal morbidity; co-amoxiclav is avoided due to NEC risk. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

explanation.summary: For preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) before 34 weeks, the aim is expectant management with corticosteroids (24-34+6 weeks), magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection under 30 weeks, and latency antibiotics. RANZCOG endorses oral erythromycin 250 mg 4 times daily for 10 days (or until delivery) based on the ORACLE I trial - prolongs pregnancy, reduces chorioamnionitis and reduces neonatal morbidity. Co-amoxiclav is avoided due to increased NEC risk. GBS-positive women receive intrapartum penicillin as well. Delivery is planned by 37 weeks or earlier for infection, foetal compromise or maternal indication.
key_points: Erythromycin latency antibiotics are the ORACLE I standard.
Co-amoxiclav is avoided due to increased NEC risk.
Steroids 24-34+6 weeks and magnesium under 30 weeks.
Deliver by 37 weeks or earlier if complications arise.
explanation.pearls: PPROM before 34 weeks: oral erythromycin 250 mg QID for 10 days (or until delivery), corticosteroids, magnesium under 30 weeks; avoid co-amoxiclav due to NEC signal.

sources.label: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida presents at 32+4 weeks with 6 hours of steady right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. Her booking blood pressure was 110/68 and today it is 138/86, then 132/82 on repeat 15 minutes later. She has no visual disturbance, headache or peripheral oedema. Urine dipstick shows trace protein and spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is 24 mg/mmol.

The obstetric registrar wondered aloud about biliary colic and requested an abdominal ultrasound which showed a normal gallbladder without stones and an unremarkable liver. Her platelet count 4 weeks ago was 245 x10^9/L. She has had no PV bleeding and the CTG is reactive. She feels foetal movements normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, foetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, no papilloedema, no clonus, mild RUQ tenderness without guarding, no peripheral oedema; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-450); ALT 210 U/L (<40); AST 240 U/L (<40); LDH 620 U/L (<250); haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L; spot urine PCR 24 mg/mmol; blood film with schistocytes; INR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis driving your management plan?

options.text: HELLP syndrome with delivery planned once corticosteroids are commenced and BP controlled
options.rationale: Platelets under 100, LDH raised with low haptoglobin and schistocytes plus AST/ALT above 70 meets Tennessee HELLP criteria even without severe hypertension or heavy proteinuria; delivery is the definitive treatment. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy with plans for immediate broad hepatic support and delivery
options.rationale: AFLP typically shows hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, coagulopathy with markedly raised INR and normal platelets initially; her INR is normal and haemolysis features fit HELLP. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Symptomatic gallstone pancreatitis given RUQ pain and elevated liver enzymes on presentation
options.rationale: Gallbladder is normal and lipase was not raised; thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis fit HELLP rather than pancreatitis. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Isolated pregnancy-related idiopathic thrombocytopenia (gestational) with likely spontaneous resolution
options.rationale: Gestational thrombocytopenia rarely drops below 100 and does not cause haemolysis or transaminitis; her biochemistry fits HELLP. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Viral hepatitis with expectant management and monitoring of foetal wellbeing over the next week
options.rationale: Viral hepatitis presents with much higher ALT/AST (thousands), positive viral serology and no MAHA; the picture is HELLP. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is a variant of pre-eclampsia defined by haemolysis (LDH raised, haptoglobin low, schistocytes on blood film), elevated liver enzymes (AST or ALT over 70) and low platelets (under 100 x10^9/L). Up to 15 to 20 percent of HELLP cases occur without severe hypertension or proteinuria; failure to recognise this atypical presentation delays delivery. Definitive management is expedited delivery once maternal stabilised: corticosteroids for foetal lung maturation before 34 weeks, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and blood product support (platelets under 50 for caesarean, under 20 for vaginal delivery). Watch for subcapsular liver haematoma and DIC as complications.
key_points: Tennessee HELLP: platelets <100, LDH >600 or haemolysis, AST/ALT >70.
Up to 20 percent of HELLP has minimal hypertension or proteinuria.
Delivery is definitive treatment; steroids for lung maturity.
Complications include DIC and subcapsular liver haematoma.
explanation.pearls: New RUQ pain in the third trimester with platelets 82, LDH 620 and AST 240 is HELLP even at BP 132/82; give steroids, magnesium and plan delivery within 48 hours.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 3 months of vague abdominal bloating and early satiety. She has no vaginal bleeding, no bowel disturbance and no urinary symptoms. Her last menstrual period was 12 years ago. Her mother had breast cancer at age 71 and her paternal aunt had ovarian cancer at age 58. She has no BRCA testing.

You arrange a pelvic ultrasound which shows a 6.2 cm left adnexal mass with 3 solid nodular papillary projections greater than 3 mm, thick internal septations and moderate colour flow. There is no free fluid and the right ovary is atrophic. Serum CA125 is 88 kU/L, serum HE4 elevated, and calculated risk of malignancy index (RMI) is 528.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild lower abdominal fullness, no ascites, no palpable mass; bimanual exam confirms left adnexal fullness
data_table.Investigations: TVS: 6.2 cm left adnexal mass with 3 papillary projections and thick septations; CA125 88 kU/L (<35); HE4 raised; RMI 528; family history as above

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 3 months to observe any change in the mass or serum CA125 rise
options.rationale: Interval observation of a complex postmenopausal mass with RMI over 200 delays definitive diagnosis of malignancy and worsens survival. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for surgical staging as the primary management
options.rationale: RMI over 200 with complex ultrasound morphology and family history mandates referral to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary service, not to a general gynaecologist. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Referral to a general gynaecologist for laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy on the next list
options.rationale: Laparoscopic cystectomy risks intraoperative rupture and upstaging in an RMI 528 mass; specialist oncology referral is required. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Percutaneous ultrasound guided biopsy of the adnexal mass by an interventional radiologist
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of a suspicious ovarian mass risks intraperitoneal seeding and upstaging; primary surgical staging is preferred. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Empirical neoadjuvant carboplatin plus paclitaxel chemotherapy before any surgical intervention
options.rationale: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a valid pathway for high-volume disease but must be initiated by gynaecological oncology after histological confirmation. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

explanation.summary: The Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology score (multilocular, solid areas, bilaterality, ascites, intra-abdominal metastases) and CA125 to triage adnexal masses. RMI over 200 identifies high risk of ovarian cancer and warrants referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for primary surgical staging, ideally by a subspecialist. Percutaneous biopsy risks upstaging via seeding and is avoided when primary surgery is feasible. Family history strengthens the case for genetic counselling and BRCA testing. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may replace primary debulking in selected high-volume disease after histological confirmation.
key_points: RMI over 200 refers to a gynae oncology centre.
Percutaneous biopsy risks seeding; avoid when primary surgery feasible.
Genetic counselling for a strong family history.
Postmenopausal complex mass is malignancy until proven otherwise.
explanation.pearls: RMI 528 in a postmenopausal woman with papillary projections needs direct gynae-oncology referral for primary staging surgery; do not biopsy percutaneously and do not defer for interval imaging.

sources.label: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

stem:
A 52-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been maintained on lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte for 18 years with excellent mood control and no admissions in the last decade. He also takes atorvastatin 20 mg for hypercholesterolaemia. His lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0). His eGFR has declined progressively: 78 mL/min/1.73 m2 four years ago, 62 two years ago, and 48 today.

He is asymptomatic and works full-time. He has no polyuria, oedema or dyspnoea. Blood pressure and urinary sediment are normal. Urine albumin/creatinine ratio is 1.5 mg/mmol. He is anxious about changing his medication because his last three relapses on other agents required hospital admission. He has never taken sodium valproate and previously failed carbamazepine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, euthymic mood, no thought disorder, no tremor, no ataxia
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0); eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2 (progressive fall from 78); serum creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110); urine albumin/creatinine 1.5 mg/mmol; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his medication management?

options.text: Reduce lithium to 450 mg nocte in the community and target a serum level of 0.4 mmol/L
options.rationale: Sub-therapeutic lithium levels risk relapse without necessarily arresting renal decline; specialist joint review is required before dose reduction. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Continue current dose unchanged and repeat renal function testing again in 12 months
options.rationale: Watching an eGFR that has fallen 30 mL/min over 4 years risks reaching dialysis-dependent CKD; specialist review is warranted now, not deferred a year. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Refer to renal and psychiatric services to plan a slow lithium taper and alternative selection
options.rationale: Progressive decline to CKD stage 3b (eGFR 48) with a rate that suggests lithium nephrotoxicity warrants joint psychiatric-renal review before further decline compromises future options. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Ceasing lithium abruptly to arrest the fall in renal function and starting oral olanzapine
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries high relapse risk within 6 months; any change requires slow taper over months with cover from a well-planned alternative. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Add amiloride 5 mg daily to preserve renal tubular function without stopping lithium therapy
options.rationale: Amiloride helps lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not chronic interstitial nephropathy; it does not address progressive CKD in this scenario. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium therapy (typically over 10 years) causes chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy in a subset of patients, presenting as slowly progressive CKD. Once eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, joint renal and psychiatric review is recommended; below 45 the risk of dialysis dependence rises and lithium should usually be tapered under psychiatric guidance with an alternative mood stabiliser. Alternatives after lithium failure or intolerance include sodium valproate (avoid in women of childbearing age), lamotrigine (better for bipolar depression), quetiapine, or olanzapine, tailored to the individual. Abrupt lithium cessation causes rebound mania and should always be avoided; taper over at least 4 weeks.
key_points: Long-term lithium can cause chronic interstitial nephropathy.
eGFR under 60: joint renal and psychiatric planning.
eGFR under 45: usually taper lithium with alternative cover.
Never stop lithium abruptly; rebound mania is a real risk.
explanation.pearls: Progressive fall in eGFR to 48 in an 18-year lithium user needs specialist psych/renal referral for a planned slow taper and alternative agent; abrupt cessation causes rebound mania within 6 months.
